claim: Clupeiformes represents an early diverging clade of the otomorpha.
source: Clupeiformes represents an early diverging clade of the otomorpha (Near et al., 2012) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Near et al., 2012

claim: The genome size for herring has been estimated at ~850 Mb.
source: The genome size for herring has been estimated at ~850 Mb (Hinegardner and Rosen, 1972; Ida et al., 1991; Ohno et al., 1969) with no recent whole genome duplications reported.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: No recent whole genome duplications have been reported in herring.
source: The genome size for herring has been estimated at ~850 Mb (Hinegardner and Rosen, 1972; Ida et al., 1991; Ohno et al., 1969) with no recent whole genome duplications reported.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge from literature

claim: The herring genome assembly is 808 Mb in size.
source: The 808 Mb assembly had a scaffold N50 of 1.84 Mb with 23,336 predicted coding gene models.
evidence: Based on genome assembly data generated in this study

claim: The herring genome assembly has a scaffold N50 of 1.84 Mb.
source: The 808 Mb assembly had a scaffold N50 of 1.84 Mb with 23,336 predicted coding gene models.
evidence: Based on genome assembly data generated in this study

claim: The herring genome contains 23,336 predicted coding gene models.
source: The 808 Mb assembly had a scaffold N50 of 1.84 Mb with 23,336 predicted coding gene models.
evidence: Based on genome annotation data generated in this study

claim: The herring genome assembly showed a high degree of completeness based on RNAseq alignments, core gene analyses and comparisons to other fish gene sets.
source: It showed a high degree of completeness based on RNAseq alignments, core gene analyses and comparisons to other fish gene sets (Table 1, Supplementary files 2, 3A–D, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Based on multiple analyses performed in this study

claim: The GC content of the herring genome is 44%.
source: The GC content was 44%, and repetitive elements made up 31% of the assembly (Table 1).
evidence: Based on genome assembly analysis

claim: Repetitive elements make up 31% of the herring genome assembly.
source: The GC content was 44%, and repetitive elements made up 31% of the assembly (Table 1).
evidence: Based on genome assembly analysis

claim: Synthetic long reads dramatically improved the discovery of indels larger than 30 bp compared to short Illumina reads.
source: Alignments of synthetic long reads (SLRs; Illumina) failed to significantly improve the assembly due to coincidental gaps between the assembly and the SLRs, but proved useful in phasing parental alleles (Materials and methods; Figure 2—figure supplements 3–4) and dramatically improved the discovery of indels larger than 30 bp compared to short Illumina reads (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: Based on comparison of indel detection using different sequencing technologies

claim: 150 endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) were identified in the herring genome, constituting ~0.14% of the genomic sequence.
source: We identified 150 endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) constituting ~0.14% of the genomic sequence but none included open reading frames in all gag, pol and env genes (Supplementary file 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Based on ERV detection analysis in this study

claim: None of the identified herring ERVs included open reading frames in all gag, pol and env genes.
source: We identified 150 endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) constituting ~0.14% of the genomic sequence but none included open reading frames in all gag, pol and env genes (Supplementary file 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Based on ERV analysis in this study

claim: Whole genome pooled sequencing was done using 20 population samples of herring from the Baltic Sea, Skagerrak, Kattegat, North Sea, Atlantic Ocean and Pacific Ocean.
source: Whole genome pooled sequencing was done using 20 population samples of herring from the Baltic Sea, Skagerrak, Kattegat, North Sea, Atlantic Ocean and Pacific Ocean (Figure 1A; Table 2); the latter sample represents the closely related Pacific herring (Clupea pallasii).
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: Each pool comprised 47–100 fish and was sequenced to ~30x coverage.
source: Each pool comprised 47–100 fish and was sequenced to ~30x coverage.
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: 16 fish (eight Baltic and eight Atlantic herring) were sequenced individually to ~10x coverage.
source: Furthermore, 16 fish, eight Baltic and eight Atlantic herring (Table 2), were sequenced individually to ~10x coverage.
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: 8.83 million SNPs were found when Pacific herring was included in the analysis.
source: We found 8.83 million SNPs when Pacific herring was included and 6.04 million among Atlantic and Baltic herring.
evidence: Based on SNP calling from resequencing data

claim: 6.04 million SNPs were found among Atlantic and Baltic herring.
source: We found 8.83 million SNPs when Pacific herring was included and 6.04 million among Atlantic and Baltic herring.
evidence: Based on SNP calling from resequencing data

claim: Average nucleotide diversity in herring was estimated at one heterozygous site per 309 bp, giving a nucleotide diversity of 0.32%.
source: The estimate was one heterozygous site per 309 bp, giving a nucleotide diversity of 0.32%; no estimate based on the 16 herring sequenced individually deviated significantly from this value and there was no significant difference between Atlantic and Baltic herring.
evidence: Based on analysis of heterozygous sites in the reference individual

claim: There was no significant difference in nucleotide diversity between Atlantic and Baltic herring.
source: The estimate was one heterozygous site per 309 bp, giving a nucleotide diversity of 0.32%; no estimate based on the 16 herring sequenced individually deviated significantly from this value and there was no significant difference between Atlantic and Baltic herring.
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of nucleotide diversity estimates

claim: Average linkage disequilibrium (r2) falls to 0.1 at a distance of 100 base pairs in herring.
source: The average decay of linkage disequilibrium between loci was very steep, with average r2 falling to 0.1 at a distance of 100 base pairs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on linkage disequilibrium analysis

claim: The allele frequency distribution in herring deviated significantly from the one expected for selectively neutral alleles at genetic equilibrium (p<2x10-16).
source: The allele frequency distribution deviated significantly from the one expected for selectively neutral alleles at genetic equilibrium (p<2x10-16, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test), due to an excess of rare alleles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) consistent with population expansion.
evidence: Based on Kolmogorov-Smirnov test comparing observed and expected allele frequency distributions

claim: The deviation in allele frequency distribution is due to an excess of rare alleles consistent with population expansion.
source: The allele frequency distribution deviated significantly from the one expected for selectively neutral alleles at genetic equilibrium (p<2x10-16, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test), due to an excess of rare alleles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) consistent with population expansion.
evidence: Based on interpretation of allele frequency distribution pattern

claim: The genome-wide distribution of Tajima's D shows a global shift towards negative values (mean=−0.57 ± 0.01).
source: The result is supported by the genome-wide distribution of Tajima's D, which shows a global shift towards negative values (mean=−0.57 ± 0.01; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Based on Tajima's D calculation across the genome

claim: Demographic analysis confirmed that herring have experienced a five- to ten-fold expansion in effective population size.
source: A demographic analysis using the diCal software (Sheehan et al., 2013) confirmed that herring have experienced an expansion in effective population size, roughly five- to ten-fold, and that the current Ne is on the order of 106 individuals (Figure 1B); the results for Baltic and Atlantic herring were essentially identical.
evidence: Based on demographic analysis using diCal software

claim: The current effective population size (Ne) of herring is on the order of 106 individuals.
source: A demographic analysis using the diCal software (Sheehan et al., 2013) confirmed that herring have experienced an expansion in effective population size, roughly five- to ten-fold, and that the current Ne is on the order of 106 individuals (Figure 1B); the results for Baltic and Atlantic herring were essentially identical.
evidence: Based on demographic analysis using diCal software

claim: The effective population size minimum in herring occurred at around one to two million years ago, after the onset of the Quaternary ice age.
source: The result indicates that the effective population size minimum occurred at around one to two MYA, after the onset of the Quaternary ice age.
evidence: Based on interpretation of demographic analysis results

claim: There is a large phylogenetic distance between Pacific and Atlantic herring.
source: The neighbor-joining phylogenetic tree including Atlantic, Baltic and Pacific herring shows a large phylogenetic distance between Pacific and Atlantic herring, as compared with the tiny genetic divergence among samples of Atlantic and Baltic herring (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic tree analysis

claim: There is tiny genetic divergence among samples of Atlantic and Baltic herring.
source: The neighbor-joining phylogenetic tree including Atlantic, Baltic and Pacific herring shows a large phylogenetic distance between Pacific and Atlantic herring, as compared with the tiny genetic divergence among samples of Atlantic and Baltic herring (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic tree analysis

claim: The split between Atlantic and Pacific herring occurred approximately 2.2 million years ago.
source: We estimated the split between Atlantic and Pacific herring to ~2.2 million years ago based on mtDNA cytochrome B sequence divergence.
evidence: Based on molecular clock analysis of mtDNA cytochrome B sequence divergence

claim: The phylogenetic tree is consistent with minute differentiation at selectively neutral loci in Atlantic herring.
source: The phylogenetic tree is consistent with minute differentiation at selectively neutral loci in Atlantic herring (Ryman et al., 1984; Lamichhaney et al., 2012); all subpopulations in the Eastern North Atlantic may have expanded from a common ancestral population after the last glaciation as indicated by demographic analysis (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic tree analysis and comparison with previous studies

claim: All subpopulations in the Eastern North Atlantic may have expanded from a common ancestral population after the last glaciation.
source: The phylogenetic tree is consistent with minute differentiation at selectively neutral loci in Atlantic herring (Ryman et al., 1984; Lamichhaney et al., 2012); all subpopulations in the Eastern North Atlantic may have expanded from a common ancestral population after the last glaciation as indicated by demographic analysis (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on inference from phylogenetic and demographic analyses

claim: Samples from the Baltic Sea cluster on one half while samples from marine waters cluster on the other half of the phylogenetic tree.
source: Samples from the Baltic Sea cluster on one half while samples from marine waters cluster on the other half of the tree.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic tree analysis

claim: Two autumn-spawning populations from the Baltic Sea (BÄH and BF) are located at intermediate positions in the phylogenetic tree, indicating that autumn-spawning herring are genetically distinct from spring- and summer-spawning herring.
source: Only three populations are located at intermediate positions. Two of these are autumn-spawners from the Baltic Sea (BÄH and BF), indicating that autumn-spawning herring are genetically distinct from spring- and summer-spawning herring.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic tree analysis and interpretation

claim: Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus harengus) and Baltic herring (Clupea harengus membras) were classified as subspecies by Linnaeus in 1761.
source: The Atlantic (Clupea harengus harengus) and Baltic herring (Clupea harengus membras) were classified as subspecies by Linnaeus (1761) in the 18th century.
evidence: Historical taxonomic classification cited from Linnaeus

claim: Atlantic and Baltic herring are adapted to strikingly different environments, particularly regarding salinity.
source: They are adapted to strikingly different environments, in particular regarding salinity that ranges from 2–3‰ in the Gulf of Bothnia to 12‰ in Southern Baltic Sea, whereas salinity in Kattegat, Skagerrak, North Sea and Atlantic Ocean is in the range 20‰–35‰ (Figure 1A; Table 2).
evidence: Based on environmental data from sampling locations

claim: Salinity ranges from 2–3‰ in the Gulf of Bothnia to 12‰ in Southern Baltic Sea.
source: They are adapted to strikingly different environments, in particular regarding salinity that ranges from 2–3‰ in the Gulf of Bothnia to 12‰ in Southern Baltic Sea, whereas salinity in Kattegat, Skagerrak, North Sea and Atlantic Ocean is in the range 20‰–35‰ (Figure 1A; Table 2).
evidence: Based on environmental data from sampling locations

claim: Salinity in Kattegat, Skagerrak, North Sea and Atlantic Ocean is in the range 20‰–35‰.
source: They are adapted to strikingly different environments, in particular regarding salinity that ranges from 2–3‰ in the Gulf of Bothnia to 12‰ in Southern Baltic Sea, whereas salinity in Kattegat, Skagerrak, North Sea and Atlantic Ocean is in the range 20‰–35‰ (Figure 1A; Table 2).
evidence: Based on environmental data from sampling locations

claim: 46,045 SNPs showed an allele frequency difference with p<1x10-10 in the χ2 test comparing Atlantic and Baltic herring.
source: We identified 46,045 SNPs that showed an allele frequency difference with p<1x10-10 in the χ2 test (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: Based on χ2 test of allele frequency differences

claim: A conservative estimate of 472 independent loci was obtained for regions showing genetic differentiation between Atlantic and Baltic herring.
source: A conservative estimate of 472 independent loci was obtained (i) by only using SNPs with p<1x10-20, (ii) by taking into account gaps in the assembly and (iii) by using the Comb-P software (Pedersen et al., 2012) to combine strongly correlated SNPs from the same genomic region (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on clustering analysis of significant SNPs

claim: Genetic adaptation typically occurs as large haplotype blocks, often including multiple genes.
source: Figure 3A (lower panel) illustrates one of the most striking associations. For a large part of scaffold 218 there are no significant differences among Atlantic and Baltic samples whereas there are striking allele frequency differences over a 119.4 kb region; this is a characteristic pattern for differentiated regions, indicating that genetic adaptation typically occur as large haplotype blocks, often including multiple genes.
evidence: Based on interpretation of allele frequency patterns across genomic regions

claim: The position of populations in the phylogenetic tree based on SNPs showing genetic differentiation between Atlantic and Baltic matches the variation in salinity perfectly.
source: With the exception of the two autumn-spawning populations BF and BÄH from the Baltic Sea, the position of all other populations match the variation in salinity perfectly with the population samples from the North Sea and Atlantic Ocean (35‰) at one end of the tree and samples from the brackish Baltic Sea (3‰–12‰) at the other end and with samples from Skagerrak (25‰) and Kattegat (20‰) at intermediate positions.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic tree analysis and correlation with salinity data

claim: The low genetic differentiation among Baltic samples (excluding autumn-spawning populations) suggests that adaptation to brackish waters is a derived state.
source: The low genetic differentiation among Baltic samples, excluding the two autumn-spawning populations BF and BÄH, suggests that adaptation to brackish waters is a derived state.
evidence: Based on inference from genetic differentiation patterns

claim: Bayenv 2.0 analysis identified 3,335 SNPs from 122 independent regions with highly significant association to salinity.
source: This analysis identified 3,335 SNPs from 122 independent regions with highly significant association to salinity (Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: Based on Bayenv 2.0 analysis correlating allele frequencies with salinity

claim: Twenty-one of the genes in regions associated with salinity have previously been associated with hypertension in human.
source: Twenty-one of the genes in these regions have previously been associated with hypertension in human and 36 of these genes showed differential expression in sticklebacks kept in freshwater or sea water (Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: Based on comparison with human GWAS studies

claim: 36 of the genes in regions associated with salinity showed differential expression in sticklebacks kept in freshwater or sea water.
source: Twenty-one of the genes in these regions have previously been associated with hypertension in human and 36 of these genes showed differential expression in sticklebacks kept in freshwater or sea water (Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: Based on comparison with stickleback gene expression studies

claim: Prolactin receptor (PRLR) is essential for mammalian reproduction but has a central role for osmoregulation in fish.
source: Firstly, the 11 kb region in scaffold 899 (Figure 3C) contains a single gene, prolactin receptor (PRLR), that is essential for mammalian reproduction but has a central role for osmoregulation in fish (Manzon, 2002), and possibly in mammals (Schennink et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on citations to studies on PRLR function

claim: A 4 kb region including part of the HCE coding sequence showed a massive copy number amplification that had a strong negative correlation with salinity.
source: A 4 kb region including part of the coding sequence showed a massive copy number amplification that had a strong negative correlation with salinity (Figure 3D).
evidence: Based on copy number variation analysis

claim: HCE is a protease, also denoted hatching enzyme, that solubilizes the inner layer of the egg envelope during hatching.
source: HCE is a protease, also denoted hatching enzyme, that solubilizes the inner layer of the egg envelope during hatching and adaptive evolution of this protein in relation to salinity has been reported (Kawaguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on established knowledge and citation

claim: Adaptive evolution of HCE in relation to salinity has been reported.
source: HCE is a protease, also denoted hatching enzyme, that solubilizes the inner layer of the egg envelope during hatching and adaptive evolution of this protein in relation to salinity has been reported (Kawaguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on citation to Kawaguchi et al., 2013

claim: No coding changes were found in HCE in herring, implying altered transcriptional regulation.
source: In herring, we found no coding changes implying altered transcriptional regulation.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and inference about mechanism

claim: Massive amplification of the HCE promoter region is expected to alter gene expression.
source: In fact, massive amplification of the promoter region is expected to alter gene expression.
evidence: Based on inference from copy number variation data

claim: A ~65 kb region downstream of SLC12A3 shows strong correlation with salinity.
source: Thirdly, a ~65 kb region downstream of solute carrier family 12 (sodium/chloride transporter) member 3 (SLC12A3) shows strong correlation with salinity (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis with salinity

claim: SLC12A3 has an established role in regulating osmotic balance and is associated with hypertension in human.
source: SLC12A3, which has an established role in regulating osmotic balance, is associated with hypertension in human and shows differential expression in kidney tissue between sticklebacks kept in freshwater or sea water (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on established knowledge and citation

claim: SLC12A3 shows differential expression in kidney tissue between sticklebacks kept in freshwater or sea water.
source: SLC12A3, which has an established role in regulating osmotic balance, is associated with hypertension in human and shows differential expression in kidney tissue between sticklebacks kept in freshwater or sea water (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on citation to Wang et al., 2014

claim: Prior to this study it was unknown if spawning time in herring is entirely due to phenotypic plasticity or if genetic factors contribute.
source: Prior to this study it was unknown if spawning time is entirely due to phenotypic plasticity, set by nutritional status and environmental conditions, or if genetic factors contribute (McQuinn, 1997).
evidence: Based on citation to previous literature

claim: 10,195 SNPs showed significant allele frequency differences (p<1x10-10) between autumn and spring spawning herring.
source: We identified 10,195 SNPs with significant allele frequency differences between pools (p<1x10-10) and 69 regions with copy number variation (p<0.001) (Figure 4A); the highly differentiated SNPs represented at least 125 independent loci based on our strict criteria (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on χ2 test of allele frequency differences

claim: 69 regions showed copy number variation (p<0.001) between autumn and spring spawning herring.
source: We identified 10,195 SNPs with significant allele frequency differences between pools (p<1x10-10) and 69 regions with copy number variation (p<0.001) (Figure 4A); the highly differentiated SNPs represented at least 125 independent loci based on our strict criteria (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on copy number variation analysis

claim: The highly differentiated SNPs between autumn and spring spawners represented at least 125 independent loci.
source: We identified 10,195 SNPs with significant allele frequency differences between pools (p<1x10-10) and 69 regions with copy number variation (p<0.001) (Figure 4A); the highly differentiated SNPs represented at least 125 independent loci based on our strict criteria (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on clustering analysis of significant SNPs

claim: The results demonstrate for the first time that autumn- and spring-spawning herring are genetically distinct.
source: The result demonstrates for the first time that autumn- and spring-spawning herring are genetically distinct and indicates that genetic factors affect spawning time.
evidence: Based on genetic differentiation analysis

claim: Genetic factors affect spawning time in herring.
source: The result demonstrates for the first time that autumn- and spring-spawning herring are genetically distinct and indicates that genetic factors affect spawning time.
evidence: Based on inference from genetic differentiation between spawning groups

claim: In the phylogenetic tree based on SNPs showing genetic differentiation, autumn-spawning populations from the Baltic Sea and North Sea tended to cluster with spring-spawning herring from the Atlantic Ocean.
source: In a phylogenetic tree based on these 10,195 SNPs the autumn-spawning populations from the Baltic Sea and North Sea tended to cluster with spring-spawning herring from the Atlantic Ocean (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic tree analysis

claim: A general linear mixed model analysis revealed 17 independent genomic regions that passed the stringent significance threshold of p<10–10 for association with spawning time.
source: A general linear mixed model was used to identify which of the 125 independent loci showed the most consistent allele frequency differences between spring and autumn spawners. This analysis revealed 17 independent genomic regions that passed the stringent significance threshold of p<10–10 (Bonferroni correction, p=4.9x10-6) (Supplementary file 3C).
evidence: Based on general linear mixed model analysis

claim: Summer-spawning herring showed a clear trend towards intermediate allele frequencies at loci associated with spawning time.
source: Remarkably, summer-spawning herring showed a clear trend towards intermediate allele frequencies at all loci, most pronounced for scaffold 481 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on allele frequency analysis

claim: Summer spawners (BÄS) did not deviate markedly from FIT = 0 and in fact to a lesser extent than the spring-spawning population (BÄV) sampled at the same locality.
source: The results, based on 1,500 SNPs all showing strong genetic differentiation between spring- and autumn-spawners and genotyped individually using the SNP chip, showed that the summer spawners (BÄS) did not deviate markedly from FIT = 0 and in fact to a lesser extent than the spring-spawning population (BÄV) sampled at the same locality (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on FIT statistics analysis

claim: The data strongly suggest that summer spawners represent a distinct population rather than admixture.
source: Thus, the data strongly suggest that these summer spawners represent a distinct population rather than admixture.
evidence: Based on inference from FIT statistics and allele frequency patterns

claim: Spawning time may be fine-tuned by the dosage of alleles affecting spawning time.
source: Spawning time may be fine-tuned by the dosage of alleles affecting spawning time.
evidence: Based on speculation from observed allele frequency patterns

claim: The estimated average heterozygosity per polymorphic site across scaffold 1420 indicated a selective sweep among spring-spawning herring but not in autumn-spawning populations.
source: The estimated average heterozygosity per polymorphic site across scaffold 1420 indicated a selective sweep among spring-spawning herring but not in autumn-spawning populations (Figure 4E).
evidence: Based on heterozygosity analysis

claim: The nucleotide diversity did not show a significant difference between spring and autumn spawning groups (spring: 0.24% ± 0.004%; autumn: 0.27% ± 0.003%).
source: However, the nucleotide diversity did not show a significant difference between groups (spring: 0.24% ± 0.004%; autumn: 0.27% ± 0.003%).
evidence: Based on nucleotide diversity analysis

claim: The number of variable sites are higher among spring-spawning herring, but the average heterozygosity per site is lower.
source: Thus, the number of variable sites are higher among spring-spawning herring, but the average heterozygosity per site is lower.
evidence: Based on comparison of genetic diversity metrics

claim: A selective sweep happened at scaffold 1420 in the past in spring-spawning herring, which was then followed by a population expansion allowing the accumulation of new mutations.
source: One possible explanation for this observation is that a selective sweep happened at this locus in the past in spring-spawning herring, which was then followed by a population expansion allowing the accumulation of new mutations.
evidence: Based on speculation to explain observed genetic diversity patterns

claim: This interpretation is supported by strong negative Tajima's D-values in scaffold 1420 among spring-spawning Atlantic and Baltic herring.
source: This interpretation is supported by strong negative Tajima's D-values in this region among spring-spawning Atlantic and Baltic herring (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Based on Tajima's D analysis

claim: Genetic differences in spawning time are expected to involve photoperiodic regulation of reproduction.
source: Genetic differences in spawning time are expected to involve photoperiodic regulation of reproduction.
evidence: Based on inference from biological knowledge

claim: The strongest signal (p<1x10-120) in the spawning time contrast is located within and up to 25 kb upstream of TSHR encoding thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor.
source: Interestingly, our strongest signals (p<1x10-120) in this contrast is located within and up to 25 kb upstream of TSHR encoding thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, which has a central role in this pathway in birds and mammals (Nakao et al., 2008; Ono et al., 2008; Hanon et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on association analysis

claim: TSHR has a central role in photoperiodic regulation of reproduction in birds and mammals.
source: Interestingly, our strongest signals (p<1x10-120) in this contrast is located within and up to 25 kb upstream of TSHR encoding thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, which has a central role in this pathway in birds and mammals (Nakao et al., 2008; Ono et al., 2008; Hanon et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on citations to studies on TSHR function

claim: Calmodulin has a role in initiating reproduction following secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) downstream of TSHR signalling in photoperiodic regulation of reproduction.
source: Further, a second gene in the same scaffold (190/1420), calmodulin has a role in initiating reproduction following secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) (Melamed et al., 2012) downstream of TSHR signalling in photoperiodic regulation of reproduction.
evidence: Based on citation to Melamed et al., 2012

claim: SOX11 encodes a transcription factor that controls GnRH expression in GnRH-secreting neurons.
source: SOX11, one of the genes in the associated region in scaffold 1440 (Figure 4C), encodes a transcription factor that controls GnRH expression in GnRH-secreting neurons (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on citation to Kim et al., 2011

claim: ESR2a encodes estrogen receptor beta that has a well established function in reproductive biology.
source: Finally, ESR2a, in scaffold 312, encodes estrogen receptor beta that has a well established function in reproductive biology (Bondesson et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on citation to Bondesson et al., 2015

claim: Treatment with aromatase inhibitors altered photoperiodic regulation of male sexual maturation in sticklebacks.
source: Interestingly, a previous experimental study in sticklebacks also indicate that estrogen receptor signaling is involved in photoperiodic regulation of reproduction since treatment with aromatase inhibitors, which leads to an inhibition of the conversion of androgens to estrogens, altered photoperiodic regulation of male sexual maturation (Bornestaf et al., 1997).
evidence: Based on citation to Bornestaf et al., 1997

claim: The expression of ESR2 but not ESR1 is regulated by circadian factors in mice.
source: Also, the expression of ESR2 but not ESR1 is regulated by circadian factors in mice (Cai et al., 2008), consistent with our data suggesting that estrogen receptor beta (encoded by ESR2) is more important than estrogen receptor alpha (encoded by ESR1) for photoperiodic regulation of reproduction.
evidence: Based on citation to Cai et al., 2008

claim: Estrogen receptor beta (encoded by ESR2) is more important than estrogen receptor alpha (encoded by ESR1) for photoperiodic regulation of reproduction.
source: Also, the expression of ESR2 but not ESR1 is regulated by circadian factors in mice (Cai et al., 2008), consistent with our data suggesting that estrogen receptor beta (encoded by ESR2) is more important than estrogen receptor alpha (encoded by ESR1) for photoperiodic regulation of reproduction.
evidence: Based on inference from association data and literature

claim: A common feature for the signatures of selection for adaptation to low salinity and for seasonal reproduction in herring is the presence of haplotype blocks (10–200 kb in size) showing strong differentiation.
source: A common feature for the signatures of selection for adaptation to low salinity and for seasonal reproduction in herring is the presence of haplotype blocks (10–200 kb in size) showing strong differentiation (Figures 3C, 4C), despite the rapid decay of linkage disequilibrium at selectively neutral sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on observation of genetic differentiation patterns

claim: Few convincing inversion candidates were detected and none coincided with the regions under selection highlighted in Figures 3C and 4C.
source: However, few convincing inversion candidates were detected and none coincided with the regions highlighted in Figures 3C, 4C.
evidence: Based on mate pair library analysis for inversions

claim: Inversions do not appear to be an important explanation for the presence of haplotype blocks in herring.
source: Thus, inversions do not appear to be an important explanation for the presence of haplotype blocks.
evidence: Based on inference from inversion detection analysis

claim: The hitchhiking model predicts reduced levels of genetic diversity in the differentiated region.
source: The hitchhiking model predicts reduced levels of genetic diversity in the differentiated region whereas the haplotype evolution model implies that nucleotide diversity in the differentiated regions, even within populations, may be as high or even higher than in neutral regions because the haplotypes are expected to have been maintained during an evolutionary process.
evidence: Based on theoretical prediction from population genetics

claim: The haplotype evolution model implies that nucleotide diversity in the differentiated regions may be as high or even higher than in neutral regions.
source: The hitchhiking model predicts reduced levels of genetic diversity in the differentiated region whereas the haplotype evolution model implies that nucleotide diversity in the differentiated regions, even within populations, may be as high or even higher than in neutral regions because the haplotypes are expected to have been maintained during an evolutionary process.
evidence: Based on theoretical prediction from population genetics

claim: Nucleotide diversity was significantly higher in the differentiated regions than in random regions of the genome both within and between populations for the Atlantic vs. Baltic contrast.
source: The nucleotide diversity turned out to be significantly higher in the differentiated regions than in random regions of the genome both within and between populations (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on nucleotide diversity analysis

claim: Nucleotide diversity was significantly higher in the differentiated regions than in random regions of the genome for the spring vs. autumn spawning contrast.
source: The same conclusion emerged from the analysis of the 30 most differentiated regions between autumn- and spring-spawning herring using the samples collected at the same locality (Gävle) in May and September (Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on nucleotide diversity analysis

claim: The data on genetic differentiation in herring is consistent with the evolution of haplotype blocks harbouring multiple causal variants.
source: Thus, we conclude that our data on genetic differentiation in herring is consistent with the evolution of haplotype blocks harbouring multiple causal variants.
evidence: Based on inference from nucleotide diversity patterns

claim: The haplotype evolution model implies that the presence of multiple alleles containing different combinations of causal variants is expected.
source: The model also implies that the presence of multiple alleles containing different combinations of causal variants is expected.
evidence: Based on theoretical prediction from the haplotype evolution model

claim: Non-synonymous substitutions showed the most striking enrichment in both contrasts (Atlantic vs. Baltic and spring vs. autumn spawning).
source: Non-synonymous substitutions showed the most striking enrichment in both contrasts and showed a steady increase above dAF=0.15 reaching a two-fold enrichment at dAF>0.50 (Figure 6, Supplementary file 3E).
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of SNP categories

claim: Non-synonymous substitutions showed a steady increase in enrichment above dAF=0.15 reaching a two-fold enrichment at dAF>0.50.
source: Non-synonymous substitutions showed the most striking enrichment in both contrasts and showed a steady increase above dAF=0.15 reaching a two-fold enrichment at dAF>0.50 (Figure 6, Supplementary file 3E).
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of SNP categories

claim: The enrichment of non-synonymous substitutions must reflect natural selection acting on the protein sequence because synonymous substitutions did not show a similar strong enrichment at high dAF.
source: This enrichment must reflect natural selection acting on the protein sequence because synonymous substitutions did not show a similar strong enrichment at high dAF.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison of non-synonymous and synonymous enrichment patterns

claim: The 74 non-synonymous changes with dAF>0.50 in the contrast Atlantic vs. Baltic occur in only 29 different genes.
source: The 74 non-synonymous changes with dAF>0.50 in the contrast Atlantic vs. Baltic occur in only 29 different genes and the corresponding figure for the contrast spring- vs. autumn-spawning is 21 non-synonymous changes in 9 genes.
evidence: Based on analysis of high dAF non-synonymous SNPs

claim: 21 non-synonymous changes with dAF>0.50 in the contrast spring vs. autumn-spawning occur in 9 genes.
source: The 74 non-synonymous changes with dAF>0.50 in the contrast Atlantic vs. Baltic occur in only 29 different genes and the corresponding figure for the contrast spring- vs. autumn-spawning is 21 non-synonymous changes in 9 genes.
evidence: Based on analysis of high dAF non-synonymous SNPs

claim: The great majority (58/62) of orthologous positions identified in other teleosts were annotated as coding sequence also in other species.
source: We identified the orthologous position for about two thirds of the positions listed in Supplementary file 3F, the great majority of these (58/62) were annotated as coding sequence also in other species (Supplementary file 3F).
evidence: Based on comparative analysis with other teleosts

claim: SNPs located in the 5'untranslated and 3'untranslated regions (UTRs) showed a more consistent enrichment compared to synonymous changes.
source: SNPs located in the 5'untranslated and 3'untranslated regions (UTRs) showed a more consistent enrichment compared to synonymous changes implying that this enrichment is unlikely to be caused entirely by close linkage to coding sequences under selection.
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of SNP categories

claim: Changes in UTRs have contributed to ecological adaptation in the herring, most likely due to their role in regulating mRNA stability and translation efficiency.
source: Thus, changes in UTRs have contributed to ecological adaptation in the herring, most likely due to their role in regulating mRNA stability and translation efficiency.
evidence: Based on inference from UTR SNP enrichment and biological knowledge

claim: Both 5'UTR and 3'UTR SNPs are overrepresented at high dAF and the trend is particularly strong for 5'UTR SNPs.
source: However, an analysis based on all SNPs showing a dAF > 0.1 in the Atlantic vs. Baltic contrast and all SNPs showing a dAF > 0.2 for the spring- vs. autumn-spawning contrast demonstrated that both 5'UTR and 3'UTR SNPs are overrepresented at high dAF and the trend is particularly strong for 5'UTR SNPs (Supplementary file 3G).
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of UTR SNPs

claim: The importance of regulatory changes underlying ecological adaptation is evident from the highly significant enrichment of SNPs within 5 kb upstream and downstream of coding sequences.
source: The importance of regulatory changes underlying ecological adaptation is evident from the highly significant enrichment of SNPs within 5 kb upstream and downstream of coding sequences (Figure 6, Supplementary file 3E).
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of SNPs near coding sequences

claim: The excess of SNPs is particularly pronounced within 1 kb upstream of the coding sequence where the promoter is expected to be located.
source: Further, the excess is particularly pronounced within 1 kb upstream of the coding sequence where the promoter is expected to be located (Supplementary file 3H).
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of SNPs in promoter regions

claim: It is possible that the enrichment of non-coding SNPs would be much higher if there was a better annotation of the functional significance of non-coding sequences in Atlantic herring.
source: Thus, it is possible that the enrichment of non-coding SNPs would be much higher if there was a better annotation of the functional significance of non-coding sequences in Atlantic herring.
evidence: Based on speculation about limitations of current annotation

claim: Intergenic and intronic SNPs were in general underrepresented among SNPs showing high dAF.
source: Intergenic and intronic SNPs were in general underrepresented among SNPs showing high dAF (Figure 6).
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of SNP categories

claim: For the most differentiated SNPs (dAF > 0.50) the intergenic SNPs showed a marked underrepresentation in the Atlantic – Baltic contrast (M=-0.64; p=5.1 x 10-25).
source: For the most differentiated SNPs (dAF > 0.50) the intergenic SNPs showed a marked underrepresentation in the Atlantic – Baltic contrast (M=-0.64; p=5.1 x 10-25; Supplementary file 3E) while intronic SNPs were most underrepresented in the spring- vs. autumn-spawning contrast (M=-0.55; p=6.7 x 10-7; Supplementary file 3E).
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of SNP categories

claim: Intronic SNPs were most underrepresented in the spring- vs. autumn-spawning contrast (M=-0.55; p=6.7 x 10-7).
source: For the most differentiated SNPs (dAF > 0.50) the intergenic SNPs showed a marked underrepresentation in the Atlantic – Baltic contrast (M=-0.64; p=5.1 x 10-25; Supplementary file 3E) while intronic SNPs were most underrepresented in the spring- vs. autumn-spawning contrast (M=-0.55; p=6.7 x 10-7; Supplementary file 3E).
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of SNP categories

claim: A total of 469 nonsense mutations were identified.
source: We identified a total of 469 nonsense mutations but expect that many of these will be false predictions due to errors in the gene model.
evidence: Based on variant annotation

claim: Gene inactivation is not a common mechanism for ecological adaptation in herring.
source: Thus, we conclude that gene inactivation is not a common mechanism for ecological adaptation.
evidence: Based on analysis of nonsense mutations and inference

claim: Hundreds of independent loci underlying ecological adaptation were revealed by comparing spring- and autumn-spawners as well as populations adapted to marine and brackish waters.
source: We have generated an Atlantic herring genome assembly and used this for a comprehensive analysis of the genetic basis for ecological adaptation. Hundreds of independent loci underlying ecological adaptation were revealed by comparing spring- and autumn-spawners as well as populations adapted to marine and brackish waters.
evidence: Based on genome-wide association analyses

claim: Both coding and non-coding changes contribute to ecological adaptation in herring.
source: The data show that both coding and non-coding changes contribute to ecological adaptation and we find that haplotype blocks spanning up to hundreds of kb show strong genetic differentiation.
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of different SNP categories

claim: Haplotype blocks spanning up to hundreds of kb show strong genetic differentiation in herring.
source: The data show that both coding and non-coding changes contribute to ecological adaptation and we find that haplotype blocks spanning up to hundreds of kb show strong genetic differentiation.
evidence: Based on analysis of genetic differentiation patterns

claim: If ecological adaptation has a similar complex genetic background as human multifactorial traits, it may be difficult to reveal individual loci underlying adaptation in species with large population sizes.
source: Thus, if ecological adaptation has a similar complex genetic background, in particular in a species with a large population size where each base in the genome is expected to mutate many times each generation, it may be difficult to reveal individual loci underlying adaptation.
evidence: Based on inference from human GWAS results

claim: This study and a previous study have revealed that genomic regions harbouring a small portion of all SNPs show strong genetic differentiation in the herring whereas the rest of the genome shows very low levels of genetic differentiation.
source: In contrast, this and our previous study (Lamichhaney et al., 2012) have revealed that genomic regions harbouring a small portion of all SNPs show strong genetic differentiation in the herring whereas the rest of the genome shows very low levels of genetic differentiation.
evidence: Based on results from this study and previous study

claim: The phenotypic effects of the loci reported in herring may be small and the strong genetic differentiation may have accumulated over many generations.
source: Secondly, the phenotypic effects of the loci reported here in the herring may be small and the strong genetic differentiation may have accumulated over many generations.
evidence: Based on speculation about effect sizes

claim: There is plenty of room for natural selection to operate in a species with a large reproductive output like the herring.
source: There is also plenty of room for natural selection to operate in a species with a large reproductive output like the herring.
evidence: Based on inference from life history characteristics

claim: The data presented is consistent with a scenario where haplotype blocks evolve over time by the accumulation of multiple, consecutive mutations affecting one or more genes.
source: Although it is expected that the majority of sequence polymorphisms associated with these haplotype blocks are selectively neutral, the data presented here is consistent with a scenario where haplotype blocks evolve over time by the accumulation of multiple, consecutive mutations affecting one or more genes similar to the evolution of haplotypes carrying multiple causal mutations as has been documented in domestic animals (Andersson, 2013) as well as suggested for the evolution of the blunt beak ALX1 haplotype in Darwin's finches (Lamichhaney et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on inference from data and comparison with other studies

claim: Under the haplotype evolution scenario, the shift from one allelic state to another rarely happens through a single mutational event since the fitness of a haplotype depends on the combined effect of multiple sequence polymorphisms affecting function.
source: Under this scenario, the shift from one allelic state to another rarely happens through a single mutational event since the fitness of a haplotype depends on the combined effect of multiple sequence polymorphisms affecting function.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning about haplotype evolution

claim: It is expected that there will be selection for suppressed recombination within regions containing adaptive haplotype blocks to avoid that favoured haplotype blocks break up.
source: Furthermore, it is expected that there will be selection for supressed recombination within these regions to avoid that favoured haplotype blocks break up.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning about haplotype evolution

claim: The analysis showing that nucleotide diversity is higher within the differentiated regions than in the rest of the genome strongly supports the hypothesis that the large haplotype blocks are maintained by selection rather than being the consequence of genetic hitchhiking.
source: Our analysis showing that nucleotide diversity is higher within the differentiated regions than in the rest of the genome (Figure 5) strongly supports our hypothesis that the large haplotype blocks are maintained by selection rather than being the consequence of genetic hitchhiking (Maynard-Smith and Haigh, 1974; Charlesworth et al., 1997).
evidence: Based on nucleotide diversity analysis and inference

claim: The common occurrence of multiple non-synonymous changes in genes showing strong genetic differentiation provides further support for the haplotype evolution model.
source: The common occurrence of multiple non-synonymous changes in genes showing strong genetic differentiation provides further support for the haplotype evolution model (Supplementary file 3F).
evidence: Based on analysis of non-synonymous changes and inference

claim: The model proposed is in line with the evolution of complex adaptive alleles in species with large current effective population sizes like modern Drosophila melanogaster populations.
source: The model proposed here is in line with the evolution of complex adaptive alleles in species with large current effective population sizes like modern Drosophila melanogaster populations (Karasov et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on comparison with other studies

claim: King and Wilson argued 40 years ago that regulatory changes are more important than protein changes for phenotypic differences among primates.
source: King and Wilson (1975) argued already 40 years ago that regulatory changes are more important than protein changes for phenotypic differences among primates.
evidence: Based on citation to King and Wilson, 1975

claim: There was a highly significant excess of non-synonymous changes as well as SNPs in UTRs and within 5 kb upstream and downstream of coding sequences among the loci showing strong genetic differentiation.
source: There was a highly significant excess of non-synonymous changes as well as SNPs in UTRs and within 5 kb upstream and downstream of coding sequences among the loci showing strong genetic differentiation (Figure 6).
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis

claim: Both coding and non-coding changes contribute to ecological adaptation in the herring.
source: Thus, both coding and non-coding changes contribute to ecological adaptation in the herring.
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of different SNP categories

claim: It is likely that regulatory changes are in majority among the causal variants because there are more than 10 times as many non-coding as coding changes among the SNPs showing the strongest genetic differentiation.
source: The enrichment was clearly most pronounced for non-synonymous SNPs but it is likely that regulatory changes are in majority among the causal variants because there are more than 10 times as many non-coding as coding changes among the SNPs showing the strongest genetic differentiation (Supplementary file 3F).
evidence: Based on inference from counts of coding vs. non-coding changes

claim: At present we cannot judge the relative importance of coding and non-coding changes, partially due to the strong linkage disequilibrium between coding and non-coding changes and partially because we have no data on the effect size of individual loci.
source: However, at present we cannot judge the relative importance of coding and non-coding changes, partially due to the strong linkage disequilibrium between coding and non-coding changes and partially because we have no data on the effect size of individual loci.
evidence: Based on acknowledgment of limitations

claim: SNPs with 10–15% allele frequency difference between populations contribute to ecological adaptation in the herring.
source: We observed a highly significant excess of several categories of SNPs even for loci with only a 10–15% allele frequency difference between populations (Supplementary file 3E) suggesting that SNPs with such minor changes in allele frequencies contribute to ecological adaptation in the herring.
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis and inference

claim: Consistent with previous studies in domestic animals, gene inactivation has not contributed to adaptive evolution in herring.
source: Consistent with previous studies in domestic animals (Carneiro et al., 2014; Rubin et al., 2010), we did not find any indication that gene inactivation has contributed to adaptive evolution.
evidence: Based on analysis of nonsense mutations and comparison with other studies

claim: Timing of reproduction is of utmost importance for fitness in plants and animals.
source: Timing of reproduction is of utmost importance for fitness in plants and animals and it is well documented that climate change affects reproductive success in both terrestrial (Visser et al., 2015) and aquatic organisms (Edwards and Richardson, 2004).
evidence: Based on established knowledge and citations

claim: Climate change affects reproductive success in both terrestrial and aquatic organisms.
source: Timing of reproduction is of utmost importance for fitness in plants and animals and it is well documented that climate change affects reproductive success in both terrestrial (Visser et al., 2015) and aquatic organisms (Edwards and Richardson, 2004).
evidence: Based on citations to studies on climate change effects

claim: More than 100 independent loci show strong genetic differentiation between spring- and autumn-spawners.
source: We identified more than 100 independent loci showing strong genetic differentiation between spring- and autumn-spawners.
evidence: Based on association analysis

claim: Not all loci showing genetic differentiation between spring- and autumn-spawners are expected to control reproduction since other life history parameters differ between populations.
source: Not all of these are expected to control reproduction since other life history parameters differ between populations.
evidence: Based on inference about confounding factors

claim: Several of the most strongly associated regions overlapped genes with a role in photoperiodic regulation of reproduction in birds and mammals, such as TSHR, calmodulin and SOX11.
source: However, several of the most strongly associated regions overlapped genes with a role in photoperiodic regulation of reproduction in birds and mammals, such as thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TSHR), calmodulin and SOX11 (Ono et al., 2008; Hanon et al., 2008; Nakao et al., 2008; Melamed et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on association analysis and comparison with literature

claim: Photoperiodic regulation in fish is poorly studied.
source: Photoperiodic regulation in fish is poorly studied, but a recent study showed that the saccus vasculosus brain region is a sensor of changes in day length and suggested that changes in day length affect TSHR expression in this region in Masu salmon (Nakane et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on statement about state of knowledge and citation

claim: A recent study showed that the saccus vasculosus brain region is a sensor of changes in day length and suggested that changes in day length affect TSHR expression in this region in Masu salmon.
source: Photoperiodic regulation in fish is poorly studied, but a recent study showed that the saccus vasculosus brain region is a sensor of changes in day length and suggested that changes in day length affect TSHR expression in this region in Masu salmon (Nakane et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on citation to Nakane et al., 2013

claim: Strong signatures of selection at TSHR in chicken and sheep may reflect selection against seasonal reproduction in domestic animals.
source: Interestingly, strong signatures of selection at TSHR in chicken (Rubin et al., 2010) and sheep (Kijas et al., 2012) may reflect selection against seasonal reproduction in domestic animals.
evidence: Based on citations and speculation about selection in domestic animals

claim: The population structure of Atlantic herring has been under debate for more than a century.
source: The population structure of Atlantic herring has been under debate for more than a century (McQuinn, 1997; Iles and Sinclair, 1982).
evidence: Based on citations to historical literature

claim: The data are consistent with a metapopulation structure in which subpopulations (stocks) are not reproductively isolated.
source: Our data are consistent with a metapopulation structure (McQuinn, 1997) in which subpopulations (stocks) are not reproductively isolated.
evidence: Based on inference from genetic data

claim: Gene flow combined with large effective population sizes explains low genetic differentiation at selectively neutral loci in herring.
source: Gene flow combined with large effective population sizes explains low genetic differentiation at selectively neutral loci.
evidence: Based on inference from population genetic data

claim: Despite gene flow and large effective population sizes, natural selection is sufficiently strong to cause genetic differentiation at many loci underlying adaptation.
source: Despite this, natural selection is sufficiently strong to cause genetic differentiation at many loci underlying adaptation.
evidence: Based on inference from genetic differentiation patterns

claim: Many populations of marine fish, including the herring, have been severely affected by overfishing.
source: Many populations of marine fish, including the herring, have been severely affected by overfishing (Worm et al., 2006; Dickey-Collas et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on citations to studies on overfishing

claim: This study shows how genomic technologies can be used in a cost-effective manner to make major leaps in characterization of population structure and genetic diversity.
source: Our study shows how genomic technologies can be used in a cost-effective manner to make major leaps in characterization of population structure and genetic diversity.
evidence: Based on reflection on the study's approach and results

claim: The study has important implications for sustainable fishery management of herring by providing a comprehensive list of genetic markers that can be used for stock assessments.
source: The study has important implications for sustainable fishery management of herring by providing a comprehensive list of genetic markers that can be used for stock assessments, including the first molecular tools to distinguish autumn- and spring-spawning herring.
evidence: Based on inference about applications of the results

claim: This study provides the first molecular tools to distinguish autumn- and spring-spawning herring.
source: The study has important implications for sustainable fishery management of herring by providing a comprehensive list of genetic markers that can be used for stock assessments, including the first molecular tools to distinguish autumn- and spring-spawning herring.
evidence: Based on the results of the spawning time analysis

claim: The findings that spring- and autumn-spawners constitute distinct populations imply that fisheries management should aim to protect both populations separately.
source: Moreover, the findings that spring- and autumn-spawners constitute distinct populations imply that fisheries management should aim to protect both populations separately, which is currently not the case in the Baltic Sea (ICES, 2014).
evidence: Based on inference from genetic distinctiveness of spawning groups

claim: Spring- and autumn-spawners are currently not protected separately in the Baltic Sea.
source: Moreover, the findings that spring- and autumn-spawners constitute distinct populations imply that fisheries management should aim to protect both populations separately, which is currently not the case in the Baltic Sea (ICES, 2014).
evidence: Based on citation to ICES, 2014

claim: The study has implications for fish aquaculture due to the interest to alter seasonal reproduction and adaptation to different salinities.
source: Finally, the study also has implications for fish aquaculture due to the interest to alter seasonal reproduction and adaptation to different salinities.
evidence: Based on inference about potential applications

claim: 84% of the core genes were scored as 'complete' in the herring assembly (>70% aligned).
source: 84% of the core genes were scored as 'complete' in the assembly (>70% aligned), and only 2.5% were missing from the assembly (<30% aligned), which indicates that the gene space is well represented in the assembly (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: Based on CEGMA analysis

claim: Only 2.5% of core genes were missing from the herring assembly (<30% aligned).
source: 84% of the core genes were scored as 'complete' in the assembly (>70% aligned), and only 2.5% were missing from the assembly (<30% aligned), which indicates that the gene space is well represented in the assembly (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: Based on CEGMA analysis

claim: The gene space is well represented in the herring assembly.
source: 84% of the core genes were scored as 'complete' in the assembly (>70% aligned), and only 2.5% were missing from the assembly (<30% aligned), which indicates that the gene space is well represented in the assembly (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: Based on inference from CEGMA results

claim: Around 8% of the herring genome retains coding potential.
source: Based on this data, around 8% of the genome retains coding potential (Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: Based on genome annotation statistics

claim: A total number of 993 tRNAs with a total gene length of 73,203 bp were discovered in the herring genome.
source: Apart from the protein coding genes, we also discovered a total number of 993 tRNAs with a total gene length of 73,203 bp using tRNAscan (v1.3.1) (Lowe and Eddy, 1997).
evidence: Based on tRNA prediction analysis

claim: Only 4,838 transcripts (3,375 genes) remained with no functional information available after annotation.
source: Only 4,838 transcripts (3,375 genes) remained with no functional information available.
evidence: Based on functional annotation results

claim: The herring assembly contained 14,107 orthologous gene families.
source: We found that the herring assembly contained 14,107 orthologous gene families, 9,634 of which were common to four fish genomes (C. harengus, D. rerio, L. chalumnae, G. morhua), and 573 of these gene families were specific only to the herring genome (Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on OrthoMCL clustering analysis

claim: 9,634 orthologous gene families were common to four fish genomes (C. harengus, D. rerio, L. chalumnae, G. morhua).
source: We found that the herring assembly contained 14,107 orthologous gene families, 9,634 of which were common to four fish genomes (C. harengus, D. rerio, L. chalumnae, G. morhua), and 573 of these gene families were specific only to the herring genome (Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on OrthoMCL clustering analysis

claim: 573 gene families were specific only to the herring genome.
source: We found that the herring assembly contained 14,107 orthologous gene families, 9,634 of which were common to four fish genomes (C. harengus, D. rerio, L. chalumnae, G. morhua), and 573 of these gene families were specific only to the herring genome (Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on OrthoMCL clustering analysis

claim: The number of identified ERVs in herring is somewhat lower than in most vertebrate hosts but comparable to other fish genomes.
source: The number of identified ERVs is somewhat lower than in most vertebrate hosts but comparable to other fish genomes (Hayward et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on comparison with other genomes and citation

claim: Epsilon retroviruses such as the Walleye dermal sarcoma virus (WDSV) are typical findings in fish genomes.
source: Epsilon retroviruses such as the Walleye dermal sarcoma virus (WDSV) are typical findings in fish genomes and 8 epsilon-like ERVs could be determined by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Based on established knowledge and phylogenetic analysis

claim: 8 epsilon-like ERVs could be determined by phylogenetic analysis in herring.
source: Epsilon retroviruses such as the Walleye dermal sarcoma virus (WDSV) are typical findings in fish genomes and 8 epsilon-like ERVs could be determined by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis

claim: Three ERVs group together with the Snakehead fish retrovirus (SnRV).
source: Additionally, three ERVs group together with the Snakehead fish retrovirus (SnRV) and 51 ERVs form a large basal clade in the phylogenetic tree without known reference sequences, possibly a transition between known retroviral sequences and gypsy retrotransposons represented by Cer1 in the root of the tree.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis

claim: 51 ERVs form a large basal clade in the phylogenetic tree without known reference sequences, possibly a transition between known retroviral sequences and gypsy retrotransposons.
source: Additionally, three ERVs group together with the Snakehead fish retrovirus (SnRV) and 51 ERVs form a large basal clade in the phylogenetic tree without known reference sequences, possibly a transition between known retroviral sequences and gypsy retrotransposons represented by Cer1 in the root of the tree.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis and speculation
